 ‘No Aid for Ghost Students Act’ underscores federal role in Minnesota’s fraud fight
 Eric Rasmussen KSTP 
 --> 
 As Minnesota prepares to launch an automated system to flag and prevent fraud in college applications across the state, federal reforms are also pending in Washington.
 Legislation known as the No Aid for Ghost Students Act is now awaiting passage in the Senate.
 The bill would require an “identity fraud detection system” to be used on every Free Application for Federal Student Aid, known as FAFSA.
 Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have been calling for tighter controls since 5 INVESTIGATES documented cases of enrollment fraud where bad actors used stolen identities to apply to colleges and access financial aid.
 In 2025, Education Secretary Linda McMahon criticized Minnesota for its handling of the issue, but during a stop in Rochester last week, she acknowledged enrollment fraud largely “started at the federal level, for sure.”
 RELATED: Secretary of Education visits Minnesota, faces questions about federal funding 
 Earlier this year, the U.S. Department of Education said it began a fraud-detection process to identify “high-risk applicants” who are required to take additional steps to confirm their identities.
 “We’ve prevented about $400 million from going out the door,” McMahon said. “And that’s just over the past few months.”
 When asked how it calculated that number, the Department of Education said it has blocked thousands of student aid applications worth an average of $6,800 since the enhanced detection process launched in April.
 Minnesota State officials say they have been raising concerns with the federal government “for the past two years” about the need for “stronger identity verification in the FAFSA process,” according to a statement from Ali Pickens-Opoku, system director for Strategic Enrollment Management.
 RELATED: College debt racked up by ghost students in Minnesota is threatening the paychecks of real victims 
 “We welcomed the additional identity verification measures implemented this spring and believe they are an important safeguard for students, institutions and federal financial aid programs,” Pickens-Opoku said.
 The additional controls proposed in the federal legislation are similar to the steps Minnesota State is currently taking to set up an automated identity verification system for college applications, using one-time funding of $3 million from the state legislature earlier this year. 
 Minnesota State’s proposed legislative request would now seek $1.5 million in annual funding, beginning in fiscal year 2029, to continue operating the system.
